It is not to be punctuated so as to say: I am straitened, and afterwards it follows, having a desire out of the two, namely of being dissolved and of remaining in the flesh; which is judged from the very text of the sentence, as follows: to be dissolved and to be with Christ is far the better. Then follows: I say, having a desire, or longing, to be dissolved from these miseries, by which I am bound as if with fetters, and to be with Christ in presence. But he is what he is, because that one is God and this one, that one almighty and this one, that one unchangeable and this one; therefore it was not robbery to be equal to God, because it was by nature; as he is born, so also always born, and as always born, so always equal.
65_marg493: The same. He did not therefore beget one unequal, nor add equality to him already born, but by begetting gave it, because he begot an equal, not an unequal. Not without reason, then, does Scripture say both: namely, that the Son is equal to the Father and that the Father is greater than the Son. The one is on account of the form of God, the other on account of the form of a servant, on account of which he was made less not only than the Father, but even than himself and the Holy Spirit; and also: “Thou hast made him a little lower than the angels”; therefore he was both made man and remained God. Therefore it is very reasonable that Christ the man is less than the Father, and that the same Christ, God, is equal to the Father. For Christ, the Son of God, is both God and man: God from eternity, man in time. God, because he is God the Word. Man, because in the unity of person a rational soul and flesh were joined to the Word. For when he was the only Son of God, in order that he might also be “full of grace,” the one Son of God was made the son of man, and the same is the son of man. There are not two sons of God, God and man, but one Son of God, God without beginning, man having received a beginning.

65_marg497: Habit is the assumption of a man, like a garment which does not change what it clothes.
65_marg498: “Habit” is said of a thing that comes to a person in order to be had. Yet there is this difference: some of the things that come so as to make a habit are not changed but change, as wisdom, which makes a wise man of a fool, remaining itself whole and unshaken. Others both change and are changed, as food, which loses its appearance when it is turned into the body, and changes weakness into strength. A third kind neither changes nor is changed, as a ring placed on the finger; this kind is very rarely found. A fourth kind: the things that come are changed, not in their nature, but are in a manner formed, and receive another appearance and form, as a garment, which when cast off and laid aside does not have the form it takes when put on. For put on the limbs it receives a form it does not have when taken off; this kind fits here. And according to this: He emptied himself.
65_marg499: God the Son, not changing his own form, but taking the form of a servant, and not converted or transmuted into man with his unchangeable stability lost, “was made in the likeness of men.” He is himself the one who assumes, in assuming a true man; this likeness expresses a true man. “And in habit found as a man,” that is, by having man he was found as a man by those to whom he appeared in man. When he says: As a man, it is such as that: “As of the only begotten of the Father.” For it expresses the truth. Has not the habit, then, sufficiently signified how he had said he was made in the likeness of man, because he was made so not by transfiguration into man but by habit, when he was clothed with the man whom, uniting him to himself, he in a manner conformed and joined to immortality and eternity?

Beware how you understand the aforesaid words of the illustrious men Ambrose and Augustine, lest they be thought to contradict each other. 65_marg586: He who is not lifted up by the things he has received, who does not twist them to the use of vain glory, who does not possess alone what he has received but divides it mercifully with the needy, knows how to abound. He who, having received food, uses it not for the gorging of the belly but for the preparation of strength, and gives the flesh no more than necessity asks, knows how to be full. He who bears want of food without murmuring, and for the necessity of living does nothing by which the soul may fall into the snare of sin, knows how to be hungry.

65_marg588: Not that I seek, etc. Augustine. The gift is the thing itself that is given as a present: food, drink, and the like. But the fruit is the good works, and the right will of the giver. Whence the Lord in the Gospel does not say simply: He who receives a just man or a prophet; but he added: “in the name of a just man” or “of a prophet.” For to receive a prophet or a just man is a gift; to do this in the name of a just man or prophet is fruit. Elias is read to have been fed by a raven and by a widow. But by the raven, who was fed without being given in the name of a just man; by the widow, with fruit, who knew that she was feeding a man of God.
